claims.text: The baseline alloy is equiatomic Hf20Mo20Ta20Ti20Zr20.
The baseline alloy is a single-phase BCC solid solution.
The baseline alloy typically has yield strength above 1000 MPa at room temperature.
The baseline alloy typically has room-temperature tensile ductility below 5%.
The baseline alloy has a density of approximately 12.5 g/cm³.
Fifteen atomic percent of Hf and Zr will be substituted with Nb and Si.
The baseline composition will be alloyed with 3 at.% Nb and 0.5 at.% Si.
The specified Nb/Si addition and heat treatment will produce nanometer-scale coherent or semi-coherent, Nb/Si-rich B2 precipitates in a BCC matrix.
Nb and Si promote B2 ordering because of their high ordering tendency.
The B2 precipitates strengthen the alloy through Orowan strengthening.
Localized shear banding in the B2 phase accommodates plastic strain and prevents catastrophic brittle fracture.
Replacing Hf and Zr with lower-atomic-mass Nb reduces the bulk density.
The modified alloy will have a room-temperature yield strength above 1200 MPa.
The modified alloy will have room-temperature elongation to failure above 10%.
The modified alloy will have a density of approximately 11.5 g/cm³, about 8% below the baseline.
Aging between 750°C and 850°C ensures B2 precipitation without forming brittle Laves phases.
A total Nb/Si content above 5 at.% causes excessive embrittlement.
The strengthening-and-ductility approach requires the alloy to remain in the BCC+B2 two-phase region.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis specifies substitution of 15 at.% of Hf and Zr, whereas the intervention specifies only 3 at.% Nb plus 0.5 at.% Si and does not state how much Hf or Zr is removed. The proposed modified composition is therefore internally inconsistent and does not close to a defined 100 at.% composition.
The conditions call for strict aging control between 750°C and 850°C, while the boundary states only that aging must not exceed 900°C. This leaves the status of the 850–900°C range ambiguous.
